title: W.P No. 7875-P of 2025 Muhammad Ishaq Khan  Vs  Govt: of KP, through Chief Secretary Civil Secretariat, Peshawar, and others
text:
1
JUDGMENT SHEET
IN THE PESHAWAR HIGH COURT,
PESHAWAR
(Judicial Department)
W.P No.7875-P/2025
Muhammad Ishaq Khan son of Reayat Khan,
resident of House No.401, D-2, Zone-4, Regi
Model Town, Peshawar
Vs.
Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, through
Chief Secretary, Civil Secretariat, Peshawar,
and others
For petitioner: Syed Haziq Ali Shah, Advocate.
For respondents: Mr. Bilal Khan, AAG.
Date of hearing: 19.05.2026.
***
INAM ULLAH KHAN, J.- Through this petition under
Article 199 of the Constitution, the petitioner prayed
for the following relief:
In view of the above, it is humbly prayed
that this Hon’ble Court may graciously be
pleased to:
a. Declare the decision of omitting the
post of Procurement Specialist in the
revised PC-1 of the Project as illegal,
unlawful, without any lawful authority,
void-ab-initio and ineffective upon the
rights of the petitioner and set-aside
the same.
b. Direct the respondents to treat the
petitioner in accordance with law.
c. Direct the respondents to consider the
petitioner for the post of procurement
Specialist in the project for the
remaining life of the project.
2
d. Any other relief as may be deemed
appropriate by this Hon’ble Court may
also be granted.
2. The petitioner is a highly qualified and
experienced professional in the fields of agriculture
economics and procurement. He obtained a Master’s
degree in Procurement and Supply Chain
Management from Sheffield Hallam University in 2011
and a B.S. degree in Agriculture Economics from The
University of Agriculture Peshawar in 2008. He was
appointed as Procurement Specialist (BPS-18) on
contract basis in the project titled “Tele-Farming and
Digital Services Platform” under the Agriculture
Extension Wing, Agriculture Department, Government
of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, vide notification dated
02.12.2022, and his contract was subsequently
extended for the following financial years. The project
was initiated to modernize agriculture, improve food
security, and provide digital and AI-based services to
farmers. The petitioner served as the only
Procurement Specialist in the project and was also
entrusted with additional procurement
responsibilities for other projects of the Directorate
General Agriculture (Extension). On 06.12.2024,
during the Pre-Provincial Development Working Party
(Pre-PDWP) meeting, the project was placed under
Cost Reduced Scope (CRS), and it was recommended
that a revised PC-1 be submitted with reduced cost
and scope. While most posts were retained, the post of
Procurement Specialist was abolished. The Chief
Planning Officer of the project later requested
amendment of the Pre-PDWP minutes, stating that all
already filled positions should continue in the revised
3
PC-1. However, without making the requested
corrections, the Provincial Development Working Party
(PDWP), in its meeting dated 27.02.2025, approved the
revised PC-1 at a reduced cost, and the Finance
Department also concurred with the revision.
Consequently, on 28.07.2025, the revised PC-1 was
finally approved, abolishing the petitioner’s post while
retaining other positions. The petitioner contends that
abolition of the only procurement post in a project
involving substantial procurement of agricultural and
IT-related goods and services is arbitrary, mala fide,
and likely to adversely affect the functioning of the
project and public interest. Despite filing
representations before the concerned authorities for
restoration of his post, no relief was granted. Aggrieved
by the actions and inactions of the respondents, the
petitioner has invoked the jurisdiction of this Court.
3. The respondents filed comments admitting the
petitioner’s appointment and the objectives of the “Tele-
Farming and Digital Services Platform.” They averred
that the PC-1 of a project is subject to revision and
restructuring under the applicable policy framework
and that the petitioner’s appointment was purely
contractual and project-specific, conferring no vested
right to continuation. It was further stated that the
petitioner’s contract expired on 30.06.2025, and prior
notice was issued in accordance with the Project
Implementation Policy, 2022. The respondents further
submitted that, due to reduction in the scope and cost
of the project, several posts, including that of
Procurement Specialist, were lawfully abolished with
the approval of the competent authority/PDWP, Finance
4
Department, and administrative authorities. The
decision was stated to be bona fide and taken in the
interest of fiscal prudence and administrative efficiency,
while procurement functions could be performed
through the notified procurement committee under the
KPPRA Rules. The allegations of mala fide and
discrimination were categorically denied, and it was
asserted that the petitioner’s representations were duly
considered but rejected in the larger public interest.
4. Arguments heard and record perused.
5. It is well established that matters relating to the
restructuring of projects, the abolition or creation of
posts, financial rationalization, allocation of resources,
and revision of PC-1 are administrative and policy
matters to be decided by the competent authorities in
accordance with prevailing financial constraints,
developmental priorities, and public interest. The Court
ordinarily refrains from substituting its own opinion for
that of the Executive in such matters, particularly where
the decision has been taken after due deliberation and
approval by the competent forums. In the instant case,
the reduction in the scope and cost of the project, along
with the consequent abolition of certain posts, including
that of the petitioner, was approved by the competent
authorities, namely the PDWP, Finance Department,
and the Administrative Department. Such restructuring
constitutes a policy and administrative decision aimed
at ensuring fiscal prudence and the efficient utilization
of public resources. The petitioner has failed to establish
any mala fide, violation of law, or infringement of any
vested or fundamental right so as to justify interference
5
by this Court in the exercise of its constitutional
jurisdiction. In this context, it is pertinent to observe
that such a policy decision of the Government cannot be
assailed through the constitutional jurisdiction of this
Court. It is a well-settled principle of law that courts
cannot assume the role of an appellate authority to
examine the wisdom, propriety, or efficacy of a policy
decision, nor can they act as advisors to the Executive
in matters pertaining to policy formulation, which
squarely fall within the domain of the Executive.
Reliance in this regard is placed on the judgment of the
apex court rendered in the case of Syed Azam Shah v.
Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Cabinet
Division, Cabinet Secretariat, Islamabad and another
(2022 SCMR 201), wherein it is held that:
12. The decision of Steering Committee was not
particularized or person specific to the appellant but
it was made applicable across the board for all
Principals, Professors and Teachers in BS-20 and
above which does not seem to be discriminatory or
arbitrary but on account of reasonable classification
with rational nexus. The compass and magnitude of
judicial review of government policy is new well
settled and defined in which neither the Court can
act or represent as appellate authority with the aim
of scrutinizing the rightness, fittingness and
aptness of a policy nor may act as advisor to the
executives on matters of policy which they are
entitled to formulate. The extensiveness of judicial
review of a policy is to test out whether it violates
the fundamental rights of the citizens or is at
variance to the provisions of the Constitution, or
opposed to any statutory provision or demonstrably
arbitrary or discriminately. The Court may
invalidate laws, acts and governmental actions that
are incompatible with a higher authority more so,
an executive decision may be invalidated for being
unlawful and also maintains check and balance.
This can be sought on the grounds that a decision
arises when a decision-maker misdirects itself in
law, exercises a power wrongly, or improperly
purports to exercise a power that it does not have,
which is known as acting ultra vires; a decision may
be challenged as unreasonable if it is so
6
unreasonable that no reasonable authority could
ever have come to it or a failure to observe statutory
procedures. The dominance of judicial review of the
executive and legislative action must be kept within
the precincts of constitutional structure."
In another case titled as Abdul Hameed and others
v. Water and Power Development Authority through
Chairman, Lahore and others (2021 SCMR 1230), it
was observed that it is not the role of the courts to
interfere in policy decisions, unless it is manifest that
such policy decisions are the outcome of arbitrary
exercise of power, mala fides, patently illegal or
manifestly unreasonable.
Reliance is also placed on case of Peshawar
Electric Supply Company Ltd. (PESCO) and another v.
SS Polypropylene (Pvt.) Ltd., Peshawar and others, (PLD
2023 Supreme Court 316), wherein it is observed that:
24. As noted above, the High Court appears to
have arbitrarily interfered in a policy matters
which it should have been reluctant to do
considering that such matters concern complex
factors which have a direct impact on the
economy of the country. Where the legislature has
expressly provided an authority for determination
in such matters, in the shape of NEPRA, then,
such authority allowed to perform its functions
because it has technical knowhow owing to the
fact that it comprises members from various
technical fields. It has been held by this Court
that in cases involving utilities and economic
regulation, there are good reasons for judicial
restraint and/or judicial deference to legislative
judgment. It is not the responsibility of the Court
to regulate economic policy. The responsibility of
the Courts is limited to legal interpretation. The
Court is expected to enforce fundamental rights
reasonably and not in a manner which creates
hurdles and unnecessary complications. In the
instant case with all due respect, the learned High
Court has overstepped its jurisdiction under
Article 199 of the Constitution and, has
7
overridden the policy/framework of NEPRA which
matter is beyond the jurisdictional parameters of
the High Court. In such a situation, the learned
High Court was required to exercise self-restraint
and defer the matter for determination to NEPRA.
Reliance in this respect is placed on the case of
Elahi Cotton Limited v. Federation of Pakistan
(PLD 1997 Supreme Court 582.
6. Being so, this court is not supposed to interfere in
the policy decision of the Government. Resultantly, the
instant writ petition is found to be without any
substance and is accordingly dismissed.
Announced
19.05.2026
(M.Iqbal)
SENIOR PUISNE JUDGE
JUDGE
(D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Ijaz Anwar and Hon’ble Mr. Justice Inam Ullah Khan.
